title: Infants Generate Structured Sequences During Self‐Directed Object Exploration
abstract: ABSTRACT Whilst decades of carefully‐controlled developmental research have told us much about the myriad variables that affect infants' early cognitive development, the relationship between infants' real‐world, self‐directed interaction and their learning is poorly understood. One theoretical account of such organization comes from computational work on curiosity‐driven learning. Previous literature predicted that when engaged in curiosity‐driven exploration, infants should impose structure on their learning environment, with this systematicity unfolding dynamically as infants move from stimulus to stimulus, generating an intermediate level of task complexity. This prediction motivated the present investigation of whether infants' self‐directed object exploration exhibits comparable sequential organization. We tested this prediction in a free play task where we quantified infants' active tactile object selections as a window into their self‐generated learning curriculum. Twelve‐, 18‐ and 24‐month‐old children ( N = 53) were allowed to freely play with three novel object categories, across six trials (two per category). Exemplars in each category were drawn from continua in which neighbouring objects varied systematically in similarity, enabling us to quantify sequence complexity in terms of similarity relationships between sequentially touched objects. Infants were first presented with a prime object drawn from one extreme of the continuum, followed by the remaining four objects presented together. Analyses of infants' first touches following removal of the prime demonstrated a systematic preference for the perceptually most distant object; however, this preference depended on prime identity and stimulus set. Cluster analysis of touch sequences further suggested that infants generated systematic sequences of overall intermediate complexity. Convergent with the computational predictions, this work demonstrates for the first time that when engaged in free interaction with the physical environment, infants are neither passive learners nor random explorers; rather, they are capable of directing their own timetable for learning by imposing structure on their physical sampling of the environment.
